claim: Multiplex tandem mass tag (TMT)-based whole cell proteomics was used to perform a comprehensive time course analysis of >6500 viral and cellular proteins during HIV infection.
source: We used multiplex tandem mass tag (TMT)-based whole cell proteomics to perform a comprehensive time course analysis of >6500 viral and cellular proteins during HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of proteins quantitated using TMT-based proteomics during the time course experiment.

claim: Vif is necessary and sufficient for CUL5-dependent proteasomal degradation of all members of the B56 family of regulatory subunits of PP2A (PPP2R5A-E).
source: We focussed on proteins depleted with similar kinetics to APOBEC3C, and found the viral accessory protein Vif to be necessary and sufficient for CUL5-dependent proteasomal degradation of all members of the B56 family of regulatory subunits of the key cellular phosphatase PP2A (PPP2R5A-E).
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on experimental data presented in the manuscript, including proteomic analysis, immunoblots, and functional assays.

claim: Vif-dependent hyperphosphorylation of >200 cellular proteins was confirmed by quantitative phosphoproteomic analysis of HIV-infected cells.
source: Quantitative phosphoproteomic analysis of HIV-infected cells confirmed Vif-dependent hyperphosphorylation of >200 cellular proteins, particularly substrates of the aurora kinases.
evidence: The abstract reports the number of hyperphosphorylated proteins identified through phosphoproteomic analysis.

claim: The ability of Vif to target PPP2R5 subunits is found in primate and non-primate lentiviral lineages.
source: The ability of Vif to target PPP2R5 subunits is found in primate and non-primate lentiviral lineages, and remodeling of the cellular phosphoproteome is therefore a second ancient and conserved Vif function.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion based on experiments testing Vif variants from diverse lentiviral lineages.

claim: Remodeling of the cellular phosphoproteome is a second ancient and conserved Vif function.
source: The ability of Vif to target PPP2R5 subunits is found in primate and non-primate lentiviral lineages, and remodeling of the cellular phosphoproteome is therefore a second ancient and conserved Vif function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the conservation of PPP2R5 targeting across diverse Vif variants and the resulting phosphoproteome changes.

claim: CEM-T4 T cells were infected with HIV at an MOI sufficient to achieve a synchronous single round infection with <10% uninfected bystander cells.
source: As previously described (Matheson et al., 2015), cells were spinoculated with Env-deficient, VSVg-pseudotyped virus at an MOI sufficient to achieve a synchronous single round infection with <10% uninfected bystander cells.
evidence: The methods section describes the infection conditions used in the time course experiment.

claim: A tight correlation (r2 = 0.97) was observed between levels of Env-GFP expression determined by mass spectrometry and flow cytometry.
source: We observed a tight correlation between levels of Env-GFP expression determined by mass spectrometry and flow cytometry (r2 = 0.97) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The results section reports the correlation coefficient and references Figure 1B showing the comparison.

claim: Expression of regulatory proteins (Tat and Rev) from Rev-independent completely spliced mRNA transcripts occurred earlier in viral replication than expression of structural proteins from Rev-dependent unspliced (Gag and Gagpol) and partially spliced (Env) mRNA transcripts.
source: As previously reported, expression of regulatory proteins (Tat and Rev) from Rev-independent completely spliced mRNA transcripts occurred earlier in viral replication than expression of structural proteins from Rev-dependent unspliced (Gag and Gagpol) and partially spliced (Env) mRNA transcripts (Karn and Stoltzfus, 2012; Pollard and Malim, 1998), with Rev expression lagging Tat in our experiment.
evidence: The results section describes temporal protein expression patterns observed in the data, supported by prior literature.

claim: Vif and Nef showed intermediate temporal profiles between early regulatory proteins and late structural proteins.
source: Vif and Nef showed intermediate temporal profiles (Figure 1C), with progressively increasing Nef expression from 24–48 hr inversely correlating with downregulation of CD4 and HLA-A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal expression patterns observed for Vif and Nef, referencing Figure 1C.

claim: Progressively increasing Nef expression from 24–48 hr inversely correlated with downregulation of CD4 and HLA-A.
source: Vif and Nef showed intermediate temporal profiles (Figure 1C), with progressively increasing Nef expression from 24–48 hr inversely correlating with downregulation of CD4 and HLA-A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section describes the correlation between Nef expression and target protein downregulation.

claim: Downregulation of APOBEC3C was confirmed during HIV infection.
source: Nonetheless, we confirmed downregulation of the Vif target APOBEC3C (Smith and Pathak, 2010) and the Vpr target UNG (Schrofelbauer et al., 2005) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The results section confirms downregulation of known Vif target APOBEC3C, supported by citation and Figure 1D.

claim: Downregulation of UNG was confirmed during HIV infection.
source: Nonetheless, we confirmed downregulation of the Vif target APOBEC3C (Smith and Pathak, 2010) and the Vpr target UNG (Schrofelbauer et al., 2005) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The results section confirms downregulation of known Vpr target UNG, supported by citation and Figure 1D.

claim: The temporal pattern of UNG depletion was distinct from that of other accessory protein substrates, with degradation seen as early as 6 hr post-infection and preserved in the presence of reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
source: The temporal pattern of UNG depletion was distinct from that of other accessory protein substrates, including APOBEC3C, with degradation seen as early as 6 hr post-infection, and preserved in the presence of reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
evidence: The results section describes the unique temporal pattern of UNG depletion observed in the data.

claim: The early and reverse transcriptase inhibitor-independent depletion of UNG likely reflects the high abundance of Vpr packaged within incoming viral particles.
source: This is likely to reflect the high abundance of Vpr packaged within incoming viral particles (Lu et al., 1993; Paxton et al., 1993), abrogating the need for de novo protein synthesis.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the UNG depletion pattern based on known Vpr biology from cited literature.

claim: Progressive accumulation of β-catenin was observed during HIV infection.
source: Accordingly, we observed progressive accumulation of both β-catenin and cyclin B1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The results section reports the observation of β-catenin accumulation, referencing Figure 1D.

claim: Progressive accumulation of cyclin B1 was observed during HIV infection.
source: Accordingly, we observed progressive accumulation of both β-catenin and cyclin B1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The results section reports the observation of cyclin B1 accumulation, referencing Figure 1D.

claim: Vpu increases β-catenin levels by sequestering the ß-TrCP substrate-recognition unit of the SCFß-TrCP E3 ubiquitin ligase complex.
source: As well as recruiting substrates for degradation, Vpu increases β-catenin levels by sequestering the ß-TrCP substrate-recognition unit of the SCFß-TrCP E3 ubiquitin ligase complex (Besnard-Guerin et al., 2004).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature to explain the mechanism of β-catenin accumulation.

claim: HIV infection causes cell cycle arrest at G2/M.
source: In addition, HIV infection causes cell cycle arrest at G2/M (Jowett et al., 1995), a point in the cell cycle associated with upregulation of cyclin B1 (Norbury and Nurse, 1992).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on HIV-induced cell cycle arrest.

claim: G2/M cell cycle arrest is associated with upregulation of cyclin B1.
source: In addition, HIV infection causes cell cycle arrest at G2/M (Jowett et al., 1995), a point in the cell cycle associated with upregulation of cyclin B1 (Norbury and Nurse, 1992).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on cyclin B1 regulation during cell cycle.

claim: Four main clusters of cellular proteins were observed based on patterns of temporal expression: 29 proteins downregulated late in infection and rescued by reverse transcriptase inhibitors (cluster #1), 59 proteins downregulated earlier and incompletely rescued by reverse transcriptase inhibitors (cluster #2), 29 proteins progressively upregulated and abolished by reverse transcriptase inhibitors (cluster #3), and 49 proteins progressively upregulated even with reverse transcriptase inhibitors (cluster #4).
source: We observed 4 main clusters: (#1) 29 proteins downregulated late in infection, rescued in the presence of reverse transcriptase inhibitors; (#2) 59 proteins downregulated earlier in infection, incompletely rescued in the presence of reverse transcriptase inhibitors; (#3) 29 proteins progressively upregulated during infection, abolished in the presence of reverse transcriptase inhibitors; and (#4) 49 proteins progressively upregulated during infection, even in the presence of reverse transcriptase inhibitors (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section describes the clustering analysis results, referencing Figure 2B.

claim: Protein downregulation (clusters #1 and #2) and upregulation (clusters #3 and #4) were validated in an independent infection time course experiment using SILAC.
source: We validated protein downregulation (clusters #1 and #2) and upregulation (clusters #3 and #4) in an independent infection time course experiment, using stable isotope labelling with amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) as an alternative quantitative proteomic approach (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section describes the validation experiment using SILAC, referencing Figure 2C.

claim: The Nef, Vpu and Vif accessory protein targets CD4, SNAT1, and APOBEC3C are found in cluster #1.
source: The Nef, Vpu and Vif accessory protein targets CD4, SNAT1, APOBEC3C are found in cluster #1, where progressive downregulation and rescue by reverse transcriptase inhibitors suggest dependence on de novo viral protein synthesis (compare Figure 2B with Figure 1D, top left panel, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section identifies known accessory protein targets in cluster #1.

claim: Progressive downregulation and rescue by reverse transcriptase inhibitors in cluster #1 suggest dependence on de novo viral protein synthesis.
source: The Nef, Vpu and Vif accessory protein targets CD4, SNAT1, APOBEC3C are found in cluster #1, where progressive downregulation and rescue by reverse transcriptase inhibitors suggest dependence on de novo viral protein synthesis (compare Figure 2B with Figure 1D, top left panel, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the cluster #1 temporal pattern.

claim: The indirect Vpu target β-catenin is found in cluster #3.
source: Upregulation of proteins in cluster #3 is also likely to require de novo viral protein synthesis, and the indirect Vpu target β-catenin is found in this cluster (compare Figure 2B with Figure 1D, middle left panel).
evidence: The results section identifies β-catenin in cluster #3.

claim: Reverse transcriptase inhibitor-independent regulation of proteins in clusters #2 and #4 implies a cellular response to HIV infection or a direct effect of viral proteins in incoming virions.
source: Conversely, reverse transcriptase inhibitor-independent regulation of proteins in clusters #2 and #4 implies a cellular response to HIV infection, or a direct effect of viral proteins in incoming virions, and the Vpr target UNG is found in cluster #2 (compare Figure 2B with Figure 1D, top right panel).
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the temporal patterns in clusters #2 and #4.

claim: The Vpr target UNG is found in cluster #2.
source: Conversely, reverse transcriptase inhibitor-independent regulation of proteins in clusters #2 and #4 implies a cellular response to HIV infection, or a direct effect of viral proteins in incoming virions, and the Vpr target UNG is found in cluster #2 (compare Figure 2B with Figure 1D, top right panel).
evidence: The results section identifies UNG in cluster #2.

claim: Gelsolin and CAPG (both cluster #4) were strongly induced during HIV infection.
source: Accordingly, we found the actin regulatory proteins gelsolin and CAPG (both cluster #4) to be strongly induced during HIV infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section reports the induction of gelsolin and CAPG, referencing Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Actin cytoskeletal remodeling is required for virological synapse formation and cell-cell transmission of HIV.
source: Actin cytoskeletal remodeling is required for virological synapse formation and cell-cell transmission of HIV (Jolly et al., 2004), and gelsolin levels have been reported to control early HIV infection in macrophages (Garcia-Exposito et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on the role of actin remodeling in HIV infection.

claim: Gelsolin levels have been reported to control early HIV infection in macrophages.
source: Actin cytoskeletal remodeling is required for virological synapse formation and cell-cell transmission of HIV (Jolly et al., 2004), and gelsolin levels have been reported to control early HIV infection in macrophages (Garcia-Exposito et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on gelsolin's role in HIV infection.

claim: Marked depletion of FMR1 (cluster #1) was discovered during HIV infection.
source: In contrast, we discovered marked depletion of FMR1 (cluster #1, Figure 2D, upper panel) and TFAP4 (cluster #2, Figure 2D, lower panel) during HIV infection.
evidence: The results section reports the depletion of FMR1, referencing Figure 2D.

claim: Marked depletion of TFAP4 (cluster #2) was discovered during HIV infection.
source: In contrast, we discovered marked depletion of FMR1 (cluster #1, Figure 2D, upper panel) and TFAP4 (cluster #2, Figure 2D, lower panel) during HIV infection.
evidence: The results section reports the depletion of TFAP4, referencing Figure 2D.

claim: FMR1 and TFAP4 both reduce production of infectious HIV virus.
source: Both these proteins reduce production of infectious HIV virus (Figure 2E) (Imai and Okamoto, 2006; Pan et al., 2009), but their distinct patterns of temporal expression suggest different mechanisms of viral regulation.
evidence: The results section reports the functional effect of FMR1 and TFAP4 on HIV production, supported by citations and Figure 2E.

claim: The distinct patterns of temporal expression of FMR1 and TFAP4 suggest different mechanisms of viral regulation.
source: Both these proteins reduce production of infectious HIV virus (Figure 2E) (Imai and Okamoto, 2006; Pan et al., 2009), but their distinct patterns of temporal expression suggest different mechanisms of viral regulation.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on the different temporal patterns observed for FMR1 and TFAP4.

claim: Three members of the deoxynucleotide triphosphate (dNTP) biosynthetic pathway were depleted during HIV infection: thymidylate synthetase (TYMS), RRM1, and RRM2.
source: First, three members of the deoxynucleotide triphosphate (dNTP) biosynthetic pathway were depleted during HIV infection: thymidylate synthetase (TYMS), which catalyses the methylation of deoxyuridylate (dUMP) to deoxythymidylate (dTMP); and two subunits of ribonucleotide reductase (RNR), RRM1 and RRM2, which catalyses the formation of deoxyribonucleotides from ribonucleotides (Figure 3B, left panels).
evidence: The results section reports the depletion of dNTP biosynthetic enzymes, referencing Figure 3B.

claim: All detected members of the B56 family of PP2A regulatory subunits (PPP2R5A, C, D and E) were profoundly depleted by HIV.
source: Second, and most strikingly, all detected members of the B56 family of protein phosphatase 2 A (PP2A) regulatory subunits (PPP2R5A, C, D and E) were profoundly depleted by HIV (Figure 3B, right panels).
evidence: The results section reports the depletion of PPP2R5 subunits, referencing Figure 3B.

claim: Downregulation of RRM2, PPP2R5A and PPP2R5D was confirmed by immunoblot.
source: We confirmed downregulation of RRM2, PPP2R5A and PPP2R5D by immunoblot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section reports immunoblot validation, referencing Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vif-independent HIV targets such as tetherin (Vpu substrate), SNAT1 (Vpu substrate), CD4 (Nef/Vpu substrate) and UNG (Vpr substrate) were depleted in cells infected with both WT and ∆Vif viruses.
source: Vif-independent HIV targets such as tetherin (Vpu substrate), SNAT1 (Vpu substrate), CD4 (Nef/Vpu substrate) and UNG (Vpr substrate) were depleted in cells infected with both WT (Figure 4A, left panel) and ∆Vif (Figure 4A, middle panel) viruses, with no difference in abundance in the presence or absence of Vif (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: The results section reports the depletion of Vif-independent targets in both WT and ΔVif infections, referencing Figure 4A.

claim: Known Vif targets APOBEC3C, APOBEC3G and APOBEC3D were all decreased by WT but not ΔVif HIV infection.
source: Conversely, known Vif targets APOBEC3C, APOBEC3G and APOBEC3D were all decreased by WT but not ΔVif HIV infection (Figure 4A), and APOBEC3B, which is resistant to Vif (Doehle et al., 2005), was unchanged across all conditions.
evidence: The results section reports the Vif-dependent depletion of APOBEC proteins, referencing Figure 4A and citing prior literature.

claim: APOBEC3B, which is resistant to Vif, was unchanged across all infection conditions.
source: Conversely, known Vif targets APOBEC3C, APOBEC3G and APOBEC3D were all decreased by WT but not ΔVif HIV infection (Figure 4A), and APOBEC3B, which is resistant to Vif (Doehle et al., 2005), was unchanged across all conditions.
evidence: The results section reports the lack of change in APOBEC3B levels, citing prior literature on its Vif resistance.

claim: All five PP2A-B56 regulatory subunits PPP2R5A-E were depleted in the presence of Vif.
source: In addition to APOBEC family members, all five PP2A-B56 regulatory subunits PPP2R5A-E were depleted in the presence of Vif (Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section reports the Vif-dependent depletion of all PPP2R5 subunits, referencing Figure 4A.

claim: Vif-dependent degradation of PPP2R5 subunits was confirmed by immunoblot of HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells (PPP2R5A and PPP2R5D).
source: Vif-dependent degradation of PPP2R5 subunits was confirmed by immunoblot of HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells (PPP2R5A and PPP2R5D; Figure 4B) and intracellular flow cytometry of HIV-infected CEM-T4 and primary human CD4+ T cells (PPP2R5D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The results section reports immunoblot validation of PPP2R5 depletion, referencing Figure 4B.

claim: Vif-dependent degradation of PPP2R5D was confirmed by intracellular flow cytometry of HIV-infected CEM-T4 and primary human CD4+ T cells.
source: Vif-dependent degradation of PPP2R5 subunits was confirmed by immunoblot of HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells (PPP2R5A and PPP2R5D; Figure 4B) and intracellular flow cytometry of HIV-infected CEM-T4 and primary human CD4+ T cells (PPP2R5D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The results section reports flow cytometry validation of PPP2R5D depletion, referencing Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Transfection of Vif caused a marked loss of intracellular HA-tagged PPP2R5A in 293T cells.
source: To test whether degradation of PPP2R5 subunits by Vif was post-translational, we expressed HA-tagged PPP2R5A in 293T cells. Transfection of Vif caused a marked loss of intracellular HA staining (Figure 4C, middle panels), and the same effect was also seen in cells expressing all other PPP2R5 subunits or APOBEC3G (Figure 4D).
evidence: The results section reports the effect of Vif transfection on HA-PPP2R5A levels, referencing Figure 4C.

claim: Vif caused degradation of all PPP2R5 subunits (PPP2R5A-E) and APOBEC3G when expressed in 293T cells.
source: Transfection of Vif caused a marked loss of intracellular HA staining (Figure 4C, middle panels), and the same effect was also seen in cells expressing all other PPP2R5 subunits or APOBEC3G (Figure 4D).
evidence: The results section reports the effect of Vif on all PPP2R5 subunits and APOBEC3G, referencing Figure 4D.

claim: The Vif C114S mutant, which is unable to recruit CUL5, was defective for PPP2R5A degradation.
source: Accordingly, we found that the Vif C114S mutant, which is unable to recruit CUL5 (Bergeron et al., 2010), was defective for PPP2R5A degradation (Figure 4C, right panels), and PPP2R5A degradation by wildtype Vif was rescued in the presence of the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section reports the effect of the Vif C114S mutant, citing prior literature and referencing Figure 4C.

claim: PPP2R5A degradation by wildtype Vif was rescued in the presence of the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib.
source: Accordingly, we found that the Vif C114S mutant, which is unable to recruit CUL5 (Bergeron et al., 2010), was defective for PPP2R5A degradation (Figure 4C, right panels), and PPP2R5A degradation by wildtype Vif was rescued in the presence of the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section reports the rescue of PPP2R5A by bortezomib, referencing Figure 5A.

claim: Rescue of PPP2R5B was seen when Vif was co-transfected with dominant negative, but not wildtype, CUL5.
source: A similar rescue of PPP2R5B was seen when Vif was co-transfected with dominant negative, but not wildtype, CUL5 (Figure 5B), and knockdown of other cellular components of the CUL5 E3 ligase complex recruited by Vif (EloB, EloC and CBFβ) (Jager et al., 2012; Malim and Bieniasz, 2012) rescued both PPP2R5B and APOBEC3G from degradation, with the magnitude of rescue similar for both substrates (Figure 5C).
evidence: The results section reports the rescue of PPP2R5B by dominant negative CUL5, referencing Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of EloB, EloC and CBFβ rescued both PPP2R5B and APOBEC3G from Vif-mediated degradation, with the magnitude of rescue similar for both substrates.
source: A similar rescue of PPP2R5B was seen when Vif was co-transfected with dominant negative, but not wildtype, CUL5 (Figure 5B), and knockdown of other cellular components of the CUL5 E3 ligase complex recruited by Vif (EloB, EloC and CBFβ) (Jager et al., 2012; Malim and Bieniasz, 2012) rescued both PPP2R5B and APOBEC3G from degradation, with the magnitude of rescue similar for both substrates (Figure 5C).
evidence: The results section reports the rescue of PPP2R5B and APOBEC3G by knockdown of CUL5 complex components, citing prior literature and referencing Figure 5C.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of FLAG-tagged Vif with HA-tagged and endogenous PPP2R5D was observed in 293T cells.
source: Consistent with a protein-level interaction between Vif and PPP2R5 subunits, we observed co-immunoprecipitation of FLAG-tagged Vif with HA-tagged and endogenous PPP2R5D in 293T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and co-immunoprecipitation of untagged Vif with endogenous PPP2R5D in CEM-T4 T cells infected with HIV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section reports co-immunoprecipitation data, referencing Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of untagged Vif with endogenous PPP2R5D was observed in CEM-T4 T cells infected with HIV.
source: Consistent with a protein-level interaction between Vif and PPP2R5 subunits, we observed co-immunoprecipitation of FLAG-tagged Vif with HA-tagged and endogenous PPP2R5D in 293T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and co-immunoprecipitation of untagged Vif with endogenous PPP2R5D in CEM-T4 T cells infected with HIV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section reports co-immunoprecipitation data, referencing Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PPP2R5 subunit depletion in CEM-T4 T cells infected with HIV was abolished in the presence of bortezomib.
source: As in 293T cells transfected with Vif, PPP2R5 subunit depletion in CEM-T4 T cells infected with HIV was abolished in the presence of bortezomib (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The results section reports the rescue of PPP2R5 depletion by bortezomib in HIV-infected cells, referencing Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Degradation of PPP2R5D was accelerated in the presence of Vif in HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells, as confirmed by cycloheximide chase.
source: Finally, we confirmed using cycloheximide chase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D) and [35S]methionine/[35S]cysteine metabolic labelling/pulse-chase (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) analyses that degradation of PPP2R5D was accelerated in the presence of Vif in HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells.
evidence: The results section reports cycloheximide chase data, referencing Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: Degradation of PPP2R5D was accelerated in the presence of Vif in HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells, as confirmed by [35S]methionine/[35S]cysteine metabolic labelling/pulse-chase.
source: Finally, we confirmed using cycloheximide chase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D) and [35S]methionine/[35S]cysteine metabolic labelling/pulse-chase (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) analyses that degradation of PPP2R5D was accelerated in the presence of Vif in HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells.
evidence: The results section reports pulse-chase data, referencing Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Vif is both necessary and sufficient for degradation of PPP2R5 subunits, and employs the same cellular machinery required for degradation of APOBEC family members.
source: Vif is therefore both necessary and sufficient for degradation of PPP2R5 subunits, and employs the same cellular machinery required for degradation of APOBEC family members.
evidence: The results section provides a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: 8631 phosphopeptides from 2767 proteins were quantitated in the phosphoproteomic analysis.
source: In total, we quantitated 8631 phosphopeptides from 2767 proteins (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The results section reports the number of phosphopeptides and proteins quantitated.

claim: HIV infection resulted in marked remodelling of the cellular phosphoproteome.
source: HIV infection resulted in marked remodelling of the cellular phosphoproteome (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and analysis using the Database for Annotation, Visualisation and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) revealed enhanced phosphorylation of proteins associated with cell cycle regulation and activation of the DNA damage response (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section reports the remodelling of the phosphoproteome, referencing Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Enhanced phosphorylation of proteins associated with cell cycle regulation and activation of the DNA damage response was revealed by DAVID analysis.
source: HIV infection resulted in marked remodelling of the cellular phosphoproteome (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and analysis using the Database for Annotation, Visualisation and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) revealed enhanced phosphorylation of proteins associated with cell cycle regulation and activation of the DNA damage response (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section reports the DAVID analysis results, referencing Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 238 peptides from 192 proteins showed Vif-dependent phosphorylation changes of >2 fold with a q value of <0.01.
source: Furthermore, as predicted for antagonism of a phosphatase, almost all changes represented increases in phosphopeptide abundance, indicating increased protein phosphorylation (with a total of 238 peptides from 192 proteins showing abundance changes of >2 fold with a q value of <0.01).
evidence: The results section reports the number of significantly changed phosphopeptides.

claim: Almost all Vif-dependent changes in phosphopeptide abundance represented increases, indicating increased protein phosphorylation.
source: Furthermore, as predicted for antagonism of a phosphatase, almost all changes represented increases in phosphopeptide abundance, indicating increased protein phosphorylation (with a total of 238 peptides from 192 proteins showing abundance changes of >2 fold with a q value of <0.01).
evidence: The results section describes the directionality of phosphorylation changes.

claim: A highly significant correlation was found between Vif-dependent changes in HIV-infected cells and published changes resulting from okadaic acid treatment of HeLa cells.
source: To confirm that the observed changes resulted from PP2A antagonism, we compared our Vif-dependent changes in protein phosphorylation with published alterations to the phosphoproteome of HeLa cells following treatment with the PP2A inhibitor okadaic acid (Kauko et al., 2015). Despite the different cell types and treatments, a highly significant correlation was found between our observed Vif-dependent changes in HIV-infected cells and the published changes resulting from okadaic acid treatment (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The results section reports the correlation with okadaic acid data, citing prior literature and referencing Figure 6B.

claim: Marked activation of aurora kinase A (AURKA) and B (AURKB) was found in cells infected with WT but not ∆Vif viruses using PhosFate analysis.
source: To identify individual kinases with enhanced activity in the presence of Vif-dependent PPP2R5A-E subunit depletion, we interrogated our data using PhosFate (http://phosfate.com/), which infers kinase activity from quantitative phosphoproteomic data by examining the coordinated regulation of known phosphosites (Ochoa et al., 2016). We found marked activation of aurora kinase A (AURKA) and B (AURKB) in cells infected with WT but not ∆Vif viruses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), and confirmed this observation by comparing phosphorylation of sites listed on the PhosphoSitePlus (http://www.phosphosite.org/) kinase substrate database (Hornbeck et al., 2015) between WT and ∆Vif virus infections (Figure 6C).
evidence: The results section reports the PhosFate analysis results, citing the tool and referencing Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A significant inverse correlation was found between Vif-dependent changes in HIV-infected cells and published changes resulting from aurora kinase inhibition with MLN8054 and AZD1152/ZM447439.
source: Next, we compared Vif-dependent changes in protein phosphorylation with published alterations to the phosphoproteome of HeLa cells following treatment with the aurora kinase inhibitors MLN8054 (Figure 6D, upper panel, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) and AZD1152/ZM447439 (AZDZM; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) (Kettenbach et al., 2011). As expected, we found a significant inverse correlation between our Vif-dependent changes in HIV-infected cells and the published changes resulting from aurora kinase inhibition, whereas no such correlation was seen for control datasets from the same study employing DMSO or the PLK1-3 inhibitor BI2536 (Figure 6D, lower panel, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The results section reports the correlation with aurora kinase inhibitor data, citing prior literature and referencing Figure 6D.

claim: PLK1 protein abundance was upregulated in both WT and ∆Vif infections, with enhanced phosphorylation of kinase-specific phosphosites, but no difference between WT and ∆Vif viruses.
source: PLK1 protein abundance was upregulated in both WT and ∆Vif infections, with enhanced phosphorylation of kinase-specific phosphosites, but no difference between WT and ∆Vif viruses (Figure 6E, left panels, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The results section reports the PLK1 data, referencing Figure 6E.

claim: Aurora kinases were upregulated equally in WT and ∆Vif infections, but increased phosphorylation of kinase-specific phosphosites was only seen in the presence of Vif.
source: By contrast, whilst the aurora kinases were also upregulated equally in WT and ∆Vif infections, increased phosphorylation of kinase-specific phosphosites was only seen in the presence of Vif (Figure 6E, middle and right panels, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The results section reports the aurora kinase data, referencing Figure 6E.

claim: Depletion of PPP2R5A-E subunits by Vif is responsible for the selective amplification of aurora kinase activity in HIV-infected T cells.
source: Depletion of PPP2R5A-E subunits by Vif is therefore responsible for the selective amplification of aurora kinase activity in HIV-infected T cells.
evidence: The results section provides a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: All HIV-1 variants tested were able to degrade HA-PPP2R5A, but the magnitude of effect was variable.
source: Vif variants were tested by transfection of 293T cells stably expressing HA-tagged PPP2R5 subunits, with the proportion of HA-tagged protein degraded in transfected cells quantitated by intracellular flow cytometry. All HIV-1 variants tested were able to degrade HA-PPP2R5A, but the magnitude of effect was variable (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The results section reports the testing of HIV-1 Vif variants, referencing Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The ability to deplete PPP2R5 subunits was conserved across all PPP2R5A-E/Vif combinations, but most marked for PPP2R5B.
source: We therefore screened a diverse selection of Vif variants for degradation of different PPP2R5 subunits (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B). The ability to deplete PPP2R5 subunits was conserved across all PPP2R5A-E/Vif combinations, but most marked for PPP2R5B.
evidence: The results section reports the screening of Vif variants, referencing Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Strong and consistent degradation of PPP2R5B was found across the entire panel of Vif variants tested.
source: We therefore tested our entire panel of Vif variants for depletion of PPP2R5B, and found strong and consistent degradation (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The results section reports the testing of all Vif variants for PPP2R5B degradation, referencing Figure 7B.

claim: SRLV Vif shares only 15% amino acid identity with NL4-3 Vif.
source: Finally, we focused specifically on the distantly related SRLV and NL4-3 (HIV-1) Vif variants. Vif-dependent antagonism of APOBEC proteins shows lineage-specificity, and SRLV Vif is unable to antagonize human APOBEC3G (Larue et al., 2010). Nonetheless, despite only sharing 15% amino acid identity with NL4-3 Vif (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), SRLV Vif was still able to associate with (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A) and efficiently degrade human PPP2R5 subunits (Figure 7C).
evidence: The results section reports the amino acid identity between SRLV and NL4-3 Vif, referencing Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: SRLV Vif is unable to antagonize human APOBEC3G.
source: Finally, we focused specifically on the distantly related SRLV and NL4-3 (HIV-1) Vif variants. Vif-dependent antagonism of APOBEC proteins shows lineage-specificity, and SRLV Vif is unable to antagonize human APOBEC3G (Larue et al., 2010).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on SRLV Vif's inability to antagonize human APOBEC3G.

claim: SRLV Vif was able to associate with and efficiently degrade human PPP2R5 subunits.
source: Nonetheless, despite only sharing 15% amino acid identity with NL4-3 Vif (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), SRLV Vif was still able to associate with (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A) and efficiently degrade human PPP2R5 subunits (Figure 7C).
evidence: The results section reports the ability of SRLV Vif to degrade PPP2R5 subunits, referencing Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Vif variants from primate lentiviruses require CBFβ to enable proper protein folding, stability and interaction with the CUL5 E3 ligase complex and mediate APOBEC depletion.
source: Whilst Vif variants from primate lentiviruses (including HIV-1) require CBFβ to enable proper protein folding, stability and interaction with the CUL5 E3 ligase complex (Fribourgh et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2013; Miyagi et al., 2014; Salter et al., 2012) and mediate APOBEC depletion (Hultquist et al., 2012; Jager et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), Vif variants from non-primate lentiviruses (including SRLV) neither interact with CBFβ (Ai et al., 2014; Kane et al., 2015; Yoshikawa et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014) nor require CBFβ to antagonize their cognate APOBEC proteins (Ai et al., 2014; Kane et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on the CBFβ requirement for primate lentiviral Vif variants.

claim: Vif variants from non-primate lentiviruses neither interact with CBFβ nor require CBFβ to antagonize their cognate APOBEC proteins.
source: Whilst Vif variants from primate lentiviruses (including HIV-1) require CBFβ to enable proper protein folding, stability and interaction with the CUL5 E3 ligase complex (Fribourgh et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2013; Miyagi et al., 2014; Salter et al., 2012) and mediate APOBEC depletion (Hultquist et al., 2012; Jager et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), Vif variants from non-primate lentiviruses (including SRLV) neither interact with CBFβ (Ai et al., 2014; Kane et al., 2015; Yoshikawa et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014) nor require CBFβ to antagonize their cognate APOBEC proteins (Ai et al., 2014; Kane et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on the CBFβ independence of non-primate lentiviral Vif variants.

claim: CBFβ but not EloB is dispensable for degradation of HA-PPP2R5E by SRLV Vif.
source: As with APOBEC proteins, we found CBFβ but not EloB to be dispensable for degradation of HA-PPP2R5E by SRLV Vif (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The results section reports the CBFβ independence of SRLV Vif for PPP2R5E degradation, referencing Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The most recent common ancestor of the primate and small ruminant lentiviruses is likely to have existed in the common ancestor of primates and ruminants, approximately 100 million years ago.
source: Accordingly, the most recent common ancestor of the primate and small ruminant lentiviruses is likely to have existed in the common ancestor of primates and ruminants, approximately 100 million years ago (Hedges et al., 2015).
evidence: The discussion section cites prior literature on the evolutionary timeline of lentiviruses.

claim: Degradation of PP2A-B56 subunits is proposed to be a primordial feature of Vif, present in the common ancestor of primate lentiviral and SRLV Vif variants.
source: We therefore propose that degradation of PP2A-B56 subunits is a primordial feature of Vif, present in the common ancestor of primate lentiviral and SRLV Vif variants.
evidence: The discussion section proposes this evolutionary interpretation based on the conservation data.

claim: The conservation of PP2A-B56 targeting strongly suggests a critical selective advantage for lentiviral replication or persistence in vivo.
source: Either possibility strongly suggests a critical selective advantage for lentiviral replication or persistence in vivo.
evidence: The discussion section provides an interpretation of the evolutionary conservation.

claim: The vif gene is found in all primate lentiviral lineages and in most of the extant non-primate lineages.
source: The vif gene is found in all primate lentiviral lineages, and in most of the extant non-primate lineages.
evidence: The results section states the distribution of the vif gene across lentiviral lineages.

claim: The ability to target cognate host APOBEC proteins is conserved across Vif variants from diverse lentiviral lineages infecting primate, feline, bovine and small ruminant hosts.
source: Whilst Nef, Vpr and Vpu are found exclusively in primate lentiviruses, Vif is found in four of the five extant lentiviral lineages, infecting primate, feline, bovine and small ruminant hosts (Gifford, 2012), and the ability to target cognate host APOBEC proteins is conserved across Vif variants from all these diverse lineages (Larue et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction section cites prior literature on the conservation of APOBEC targeting by Vif.

claim: Degradation of APOBEC family members by Vif is mediated by recruitment of a cullin-5 (CUL5) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, resulting in substrate-specific ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: Degradation of APOBEC family members by Vif is mediated by recruitment of a cullin-5 (CUL5) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, resulting in substrate-specific ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (Malim and Bieniasz, 2012).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on the mechanism of APOBEC degradation by Vif.

claim: PP2A makes up 0.2–1% of total eukaryotic cellular protein.
source: PP2A makes up 0.2–1% of total eukaryotic cellular protein (Lin et al., 1998; Ruediger et al., 1991), and whilst in many cases the relevant regulatory subunits have not been characterized, published targets of PP2A-B56 holoenzymes are nonetheless implicated in a multitude of cellular processes (Yang and Phiel, 2010).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on PP2A abundance.

claim: Published targets of PP2A-B56 holoenzymes are implicated in a multitude of cellular processes.
source: PP2A makes up 0.2–1% of total eukaryotic cellular protein (Lin et al., 1998; Ruediger et al., 1991), and whilst in many cases the relevant regulatory subunits have not been characterized, published targets of PP2A-B56 holoenzymes are nonetheless implicated in a multitude of cellular processes (Yang and Phiel, 2010).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on PP2A-B56 targets.

claim: Aurora kinase activity and abundance peak in late G2 and mitosis.
source: Aurora kinase activity and abundance peak in late G2 and mitosis (Bischoff et al., 1998; Ly et al., 2014), and PP2A-B56 holoenzymes antagonize aurora kinase functions in other systems (Bastos et al., 2014; Espert et al., 2014; Kruse et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on aurora kinase regulation.

claim: PP2A-B56 holoenzymes antagonize aurora kinase functions in other systems.
source: Aurora kinase activity and abundance peak in late G2 and mitosis (Bischoff et al., 1998; Ly et al., 2014), and PP2A-B56 holoenzymes antagonize aurora kinase functions in other systems (Bastos et al., 2014; Espert et al., 2014; Kruse et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on PP2A-B56 antagonism of aurora kinases.

claim: Aurora kinase activity is typically inhibited by the DNA damage response.
source: Conversely, aurora kinase activity is typically inhibited by the DNA damage response (Bensimon et al., 2011), and reduced activity would therefore be expected in HIV-infected cells.
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on aurora kinase regulation by DNA damage response.

claim: Vif-mediated antagonism of PP2A-B56 is proposed to sustain aurora kinase activity in the presence of the DNA damage response.
source: Instead, we propose that Vif-mediated antagonism of PP2A-B56 sustains aurora kinase activity in the presence of the DNA damage response.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the aurora kinase data.

claim: PLK1 is inhibited by the DNA damage response in other systems.
source: Interestingly, PLK1 is also inhibited by the DNA damage response in other systems (Bensimon et al., 2011), but kinase-active PLK1 is recruited to the SLX4 complex by Vpr in HIV-infected cells (Laguette et al., 2014), consistent with the results of this study (Figure 6E).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on PLK1 regulation.

claim: Kinase-active PLK1 is recruited to the SLX4 complex by Vpr in HIV-infected cells.
source: Interestingly, PLK1 is also inhibited by the DNA damage response in other systems (Bensimon et al., 2011), but kinase-active PLK1 is recruited to the SLX4 complex by Vpr in HIV-infected cells (Laguette et al., 2014), consistent with the results of this study (Figure 6E).
evidence: The results section cites prior literature on PLK1 recruitment by Vpr.

claim: Manipulation of mitotic kinases is a shared feature of the HIV accessory proteins Vpr and Vif.
source: Manipulation of mitotic kinases is therefore a shared feature of the HIV accessory proteins Vpr and Vif, and pharmacological inhibitors targeting these cellular kinases may represent a viable antiviral strategy.
evidence: The discussion section provides a conclusion based on the data.

claim: Pharmacological inhibitors targeting mitotic kinases may represent a viable antiviral strategy.
source: Manipulation of mitotic kinases is therefore a shared feature of the HIV accessory proteins Vpr and Vif, and pharmacological inhibitors targeting these cellular kinases may represent a viable antiviral strategy.
evidence: The discussion section proposes a potential therapeutic application.

claim: Replication of WT and ΔVif viruses in vitro is equivalent in permissive cell lines lacking APOBEC3G expression.
source: Replication of WT and ΔVif viruses in vitro is equivalent in permissive cell lines lacking APOBEC3G expression (Sheehy et al., 2002).
evidence: The discussion section cites prior literature on ΔVif virus replication.

claim: Aurora kinase activity controls Lck kinase location and phosphorylation at the immunological synapse.
source: Aurora kinase activity controls Lck kinase location and phosphorylation at the immunological synapse (Blas-Rus et al., 2016), and kinase-active Lck is also recruited to the virological synapse during cell-cell transmission of HIV (Vasiliver-Shamis et al., 2009).
evidence: The discussion section cites prior literature on aurora kinase and Lck.

claim: Kinase-active Lck is recruited to the virological synapse during cell-cell transmission of HIV.
source: Aurora kinase activity controls Lck kinase location and phosphorylation at the immunological synapse (Blas-Rus et al., 2016), and kinase-active Lck is also recruited to the virological synapse during cell-cell transmission of HIV (Vasiliver-Shamis et al., 2009).
evidence: The discussion section cites prior literature on Lck at the virological synapse.

claim: It is possible that Vif-mediated PP2A-B56 antagonism directly enhances cell-cell spread in vivo or in vitro in primary T cells or macrophages.
source: It is therefore possible that Vif-mediated PP2A-B56 antagonism directly enhances cell-cell spread in vivo or in vitro in primary T cells or macrophages, but it is not currently practicable to compare replication of WT and ΔVif viruses on an APOBEC family-negative background in primary cells.
evidence: The discussion section proposes a possible mechanism.

claim: PP2A-B56 antagonism may enhance HIV replication or persistence in vivo indirectly, by modulating T cell activation or macrophage polarization.
source: Alternatively, PP2A-B56 antagonism may enhance HIV replication or persistence in vivo indirectly, by modulating T cell activation or macrophage polarization (Blas-Rus et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2015).
evidence: The discussion section proposes an alternative mechanism, citing prior literature.

claim: MHC class I proteins are targeted by Nef variants of all primate lentiviruses.
source: For example, MHC class I proteins are targeted by Nef variants of all primate lentiviruses (Specht et al., 2008), and manipulation of MHC class I is a common attribute of many virus families (Randow and Lehner, 2009).
evidence: The discussion section cites prior literature on Nef targeting of MHC class I.

claim: Manipulation of MHC class I is a common attribute of many virus families.
source: For example, MHC class I proteins are targeted by Nef variants of all primate lentiviruses (Specht et al., 2008), and manipulation of MHC class I is a common attribute of many virus families (Randow and Lehner, 2009).
evidence: The discussion section cites prior literature on viral manipulation of MHC class I.
